# PyPI and pip: managing dependencies {#sec-ch-pip}

> *"If I have seen further it is by standing on the shoulders of giants."* —
> Isaac Newton (1675). In software, the giants are other people's packages.

::: {.callout-note}
## Learning objectives
By the end of this chapter you will be able to:

- explain what the **Python Package Index** (PyPI) is and how `pip` installs
  packages from it (wheels, sdists, `site-packages`);
- install, inspect, upgrade, downgrade and uninstall packages with
  `python -m pip`;
- read and write **version specifiers** (PEP 440), explain **semantic
  versioning**, and order versions correctly;
- **export** an environment's dependencies to `requirements.txt` and
  **import** them elsewhere; explain what a **lock file** adds;
- explain why choosing compatible versions is hard, and **prove** that
  dependency resolution is **NP-complete**;
- evaluate a package before depending on it, and protect yourself from
  supply-chain attacks.
:::

::: {.callout-tip}
## Course lessons covered
Theory: 12.1 *Introduction to the Python Package Index*. Practice:
12.2 *Installing and uninstalling a package with pip* · 12.3 *Selecting the
version and upgrading a package* · 12.4 *Exporting and importing new modules*.
:::

## Intuition: an app store for code

The standard library (@sec-ch-stdlib) is large, but the real power of Python
is its ecosystem: NumPy, pandas, scikit-learn, PyTorch, Transformers, FastAPI…
These **third-party packages** are published on the **Python Package Index**
(<https://pypi.org>), a public repository hosting hundreds of thousands of
projects. **`pip`** is the "app store client": it downloads a package, and the
packages *it* depends on, and installs them where Python can import them.

The hard part is not downloading; it is **choosing versions** that work
together. Package A needs `numpy>=2`, package B needs `numpy<2`: no
installation can satisfy both. This chapter explains how versions are
expressed, how tools search for a compatible set, and why that search is, in
general, computationally hard.

## PyPI and pip {#sec-pypi}

- **PyPI** was launched in 2003 (nicknamed "the Cheese Shop" after a Monty
  Python sketch) following PEP 301 [@pep301]; the current site, *Warehouse*,
  went live in 2018. Each **project** has **releases** (versions), and each
  release has **distribution files**: wheels (`.whl`, ready to install) and
  usually an sdist (`.tar.gz`, source to build) — the artifacts of
  @sec-real-package.
- **pip** (2008, originally by Ian Bicking, now maintained by the Python
  Packaging Authority) is the reference installer; since Python 3.4 it is
  bundled with Python through `ensurepip` (PEP 453 [@pep453]).

When you run `pip install requests`, pip:

1. queries the index for the project's available versions;
2. **resolves** a set of versions of `requests` and of all its (transitive)
   dependencies compatible with each other and with what is already installed
   (@sec-resolution);
3. picks, for each, the most specific compatible **wheel** for your Python
   version and platform (@exr-ch10-wheel), building from the sdist if none
   exists;
4. unpacks the wheels into **`site-packages`** of the *current* environment,
   recording metadata in `*.dist-info` so the package can be listed and
   uninstalled.

::: {.callout-important}
## Always run pip as `python -m pip`
`python -m pip install X` installs into the environment of **that** `python`.
A bare `pip` may belong to a different Python installation, and the package
then "disappears" when you run your script. In Jupyter use `%pip install X`,
which targets the notebook's kernel. And **never** `sudo pip install`: it
modifies the system Python that your operating system relies on. Use a virtual
environment (@sec-ch-venv).
:::

## Everyday commands {#sec-pip-commands}

```bash
python -m pip install requests              # latest compatible version
python -m pip install "requests==2.32.3"    # an exact version
python -m pip install "requests>=2.31,<3"   # a range
python -m pip install --upgrade requests    # upgrade to the latest allowed
python -m pip uninstall requests            # remove (asks for confirmation; -y to skip)
python -m pip show requests                 # version, location, dependencies (Requires) and dependents (Required-by)
python -m pip list --outdated               # what could be upgraded
python -m pip index versions requests       # which versions exist on PyPI
python -m pip check                         # verify installed packages have compatible dependencies
```

Note that `pip uninstall` removes only the named package, **not** the
dependencies that were installed with it. In this book's build environment we
can query the installed packages from Python with `importlib.metadata`, which
reads the same `*.dist-info` metadata pip uses:

```{python}
from importlib.metadata import version, requires, distribution
print("numpy", version("numpy"), "| pandas", version("pandas"))
print([r for r in (requires("pandas") or []) if "extra" not in r])   # pandas' mandatory dependencies
print(distribution("pandas").metadata["Summary"])
```

## Versions {#sec-versions}

### Semantic versioning

Most projects number releases as **`MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH`** following
**Semantic Versioning** [@semver]:

- increment **PATCH** for backwards-compatible bug fixes (`2.1.3 → 2.1.4`);
- increment **MINOR** for backwards-compatible new features (`2.1.4 → 2.2.0`);
- increment **MAJOR** for **incompatible** API changes (`2.2.0 → 3.0.0`).

So a project that works with `2.1.3` should keep working with any `2.x.y` with
$x.y \ge 1.3$ — if the maintainers respect the convention. Many do not
strictly; some use **calendar versioning** (`2026.11`, e.g. `pip` itself).
Version `0.y.z` means "initial development: anything may change".

### PEP 440: Python's version scheme

Python standardises the syntax and **ordering** of versions in PEP 440
[@pep440]:
`[N!]N(.N)*[{a|b|rc}N][.postN][.devN]`, e.g. `1.0.dev1 < 1.0a1 < 1.0b2 <
1.0rc1 < 1.0 < 1.0.post1 < 1.1`. The release part is compared as a **tuple of
integers** in lexicographic order (@thm-lex-order), padding with zeros — which
is why version strings must never be compared as text:

```{python}
from packaging.version import Version
print("1.10" > "1.9", Version("1.10") > Version("1.9"))       # text comparison is WRONG
print(Version("2.0") == Version("2.0.0"), Version("1.0rc1") < Version("1.0"))
print(sorted(["1.0.post1", "1.0", "1.0a1", "0.9", "1.0.dev1", "1.0rc1", "1.0b2"], key=Version))
print(Version("3.2.1").release, Version("3.2.1").major)
```

### Version specifiers

A **specifier** constrains acceptable versions; several are combined with
commas, meaning **and**:

| Specifier | Meaning | Example matches |
|---|---|---|
| `==1.4.2` | exactly | `1.4.2` |
| `==1.4.*` | prefix match | `1.4.0`, `1.4.9` |
| `!=1.4.3` | exclude | everything but `1.4.3` |
| `>=1.4, <2` | a range | `1.4`, `1.9.9` |
| `~=1.4.2` | **compatible release**: `>=1.4.2, ==1.4.*` | `1.4.2`, `1.4.10`, not `1.5` |
| `~=1.4` | `>=1.4, ==1.*` | `1.4`, `1.9`, not `2.0` |

: PEP 440 version specifiers {#tbl-specifiers}

```{python}
from packaging.specifiers import SpecifierSet
spec = SpecifierSet("~=1.4.2")
candidates = ["1.4.1", "1.4.2", "1.4.10", "1.5.0", "2.0"]
print([v for v in candidates if Version(v) in spec])
print(list(SpecifierSet(">=1.4,<2,!=1.7.0").filter(["1.3", "1.4", "1.7.0", "1.9", "2.0"])))
```

Specifiers appear in `pip install` commands, in `requirements.txt`, and in the
`dependencies` of `pyproject.toml` (@sec-real-package). For a **library**,
declare the widest range you support (`numpy>=1.24`); for an **application**,
pin exact versions in a lock file (below).

## Exporting and importing dependencies {#sec-requirements}

To reproduce an environment elsewhere — a colleague's laptop, a server, the
grader of your project — you must record **which packages at which versions**
it contains.

```bash
python -m pip freeze > requirements.txt      # export: one "name==version" per line
python -m pip install -r requirements.txt    # import: install exactly those versions
```

A `requirements.txt` file can contain any specifier, comments (`#`), and
options:

```text
# requirements.txt
numpy==2.1.3
pandas>=2.2,<3
matplotlib~=3.9
-r requirements-dev.txt        # include another file
```

`pip freeze` lists **everything** installed, including transitive
dependencies, with exact versions — good for reproducing an environment, but it
mixes your direct needs with incidental ones. A common practice keeps two
files: the **direct** dependencies you chose (loose specifiers), and a
**lock file** with the fully resolved, pinned set, generated by a tool such as
`pip-tools` (`pip-compile`), Poetry, PDM or `uv`. A lock file may also record
the **hash** of each distribution file (`pip install --require-hashes`), so that
a tampered file is rejected. PEP 751 standardised a common lock-file format,
`pylock.toml` [@pep751].

## Dependency resolution {#sec-resolution}

### The problem

Every release of every package declares its dependencies, with specifiers. The
installer must choose **one version per package** such that every chosen
release's dependencies are satisfied. This is a search problem: if the latest
`A` requires `B<2` but the latest `C` requires `B>=2`, the resolver must
**backtrack** and try older versions of `A` or `C`. Since version 20.3 (2020),
pip uses a **backtracking resolver** (*resolvelib*) that does exactly this;
before, pip installed whatever it met first and could produce broken
environments.

How hard can it be? In the worst case, **very**: it contains the Boolean
satisfiability problem.

::: {#def-installability}
## The installability problem
*Input*: a finite repository of package versions; each version $p$ has a list
of **dependencies**, each a disjunction "$q_1$ or $q_2$ or …" of versions of
some packages; a set of **conflicts** (pairs of versions that cannot be
installed together, including any two versions of the same package); and a
target version $t$. *Question*: is there a set $S$ of versions with $t \in S$,
every dependency of every member of $S$ satisfied by some member of $S$, and no
conflicting pair inside $S$?
:::

Recall that a problem is in **NP** if a proposed solution can be *checked* in
polynomial time, and **NP-complete** if, moreover, every problem in NP reduces
to it in polynomial time; no polynomial algorithm is known for any NP-complete
problem, and finding one would settle the famous $\mathrm{P}$ vs $\mathrm{NP}$
question [@cormen2022, Ch. 34]. The canonical NP-complete problem is
**3-SAT** — deciding whether a Boolean formula in conjunctive normal form with
three literals per clause can be made true (Cook–Levin theorem [@cook1971;
@karp1972]).

::: {#thm-dependency-np}
## Dependency resolution is NP-complete
The installability problem is NP-complete, even when every package has at most
two versions and every dependency is a disjunction of at most three versions.
:::

*In one line:* package versions can play the role of truth values and
dependencies the role of clauses, so a resolver that always answered quickly
would solve 3-SAT quickly.

::: {.callout-caution collapse="true"}
## For the interested reader — proof of @thm-dependency-np (reduction from 3-SAT)
This result was established for Debian and RPM packages by the EDOS project
[@dicosmo2006]; see also @cox2016 for a readable account. The reduction below
follows their idea.

*In NP.* Given a candidate set $S$, check $t \in S$, every dependency of every
member, and every conflicting pair: polynomial in the size of the repository.

*NP-hard.* Take a 3-SAT formula with variables $x_1,\dots,x_n$ and clauses
$C_1, \dots, C_m$, each a disjunction of three literals. Build a repository:

- for each variable $x_i$, a package $X_i$ with two versions, $X_i{=}1$
  ("true") and $X_i{=}0$ ("false"); they conflict (one version per package);
- for each clause $C_j = (\ell_1 \vee \ell_2\vee\ell_3)$, a package $K_j$ with
  one version whose single dependency is the disjunction of three versions:
  for each literal, $X_i{=}1$ if the literal is $x_i$, $X_i{=}0$ if it is
  $\neg x_i$;
- a target package $T$ that depends on $K_1$, $K_2$, …, $K_m$.

The repository has $2n + m + 1$ versions: a polynomial-size construction.

($\Rightarrow$) If an assignment $a$ satisfies the formula, let
$S = \{T, K_1,\dots,K_m\} \cup \{X_i{=}a_i : i = 1..n\}$. $T$'s dependencies
are in $S$; each clause has a true literal, whose version is in $S$, so each
$K_j$'s dependency holds; $S$ contains one version of each $X_i$, so no
conflict.

($\Leftarrow$) If an installable $S \ni T$ exists, it contains every $K_j$
(dependencies of $T$) and at most one version of each $X_i$ (conflicts). Define
$a_i = v$ if $X_i{=}v \in S$, and $a_i$ arbitrary if no version of $X_i$ is in
$S$. Each $K_j \in S$ has its dependency satisfied by some $X_i{=}v \in S$
corresponding to a literal of $C_j$, and that literal is true under $a$. So
$a$ satisfies every clause.

Hence the formula is satisfiable iff $T$ is installable, and the reduction is
polynomial; since 3-SAT is NP-complete, so is installability. $\blacksquare$
:::

In practice, real dependency graphs are far from the worst case, and
resolvers use heuristics (try newest versions first, learn from conflicts) or
outright SAT solvers (conda's resolver, `libsolv`); but the theorem explains why
resolution can occasionally be slow or fail with long backtracking, and why
**pinning** with lock files is valuable: it turns a search problem into a
lookup.

```{python}
from itertools import product

# A toy repository: package -> {version: [dependency specifiers]}
repo = {
    "app":   {"1.0": ["lib>=2", "util"]},
    "lib":   {"1.0": [], "2.0": ["core<2"], "3.0": ["core>=2"]},
    "util":  {"1.0": ["core>=2"], "2.0": ["core<2"]},
    "core":  {"1.0": [], "2.0": [], "3.0": []},
}

def satisfied(choice, spec):
    name = spec.split("<")[0].split(">")[0].split("=")[0]
    rest = spec[len(name):]
    return name in choice and (rest == "" or Version(choice[name]) in SpecifierSet(rest))

def resolve(repo, root):
    names = list(repo)
    tried = 0
    for versions in product(*(sorted(repo[n], key=Version, reverse=True) for n in names)):
        tried += 1                                     # brute force: newest versions first
        choice = dict(zip(names, versions))
        if all(satisfied(choice, d) for n in names for d in repo[n][choice[n]]):
            return choice, tried
    return None, tried

print(resolve(repo, "app"))
```

The brute-force resolver tries up to $\prod_p (\text{number of versions of } p)$
combinations — exponential in the number of packages; real resolvers prune this
space aggressively but cannot avoid the worst case (unless P = NP).

## Choosing packages wisely {#sec-choosing-packages}

Every dependency is code you did not write but are responsible for. Before
adding one, check:

- **Need**: does the standard library already do it?
- **Health**: recent releases, active maintainers, open issues answered,
  documentation, tests, a licence compatible with your project.
- **Popularity and provenance**: downloads, the project's link to its source
  repository, *trusted publishing* from CI.
- **Weight**: how many transitive dependencies it pulls in.

::: {.callout-warning}
## Supply-chain attacks
Attackers upload malicious packages with names similar to popular ones
(**typosquatting**: `reqeusts` instead of `requests`), or take over abandoned
projects. Installing a package runs code from its author on your machine (the
build step of an sdist can run arbitrary code). Type names carefully, prefer
well-known projects, pin versions with hashes in production, and be especially
careful with package names suggested by AI assistants, which may **invent**
plausible names that attackers then register ("slopsquatting", @sec-ch-ai-tools).
:::

::: {.project-link}
**In the project.** The phone book deliberately uses **only the standard
library** (`json`, `os`, `inspect`): it has **zero third-party
dependencies**, which makes it trivially portable — nothing to install,
nothing to pin. The moment you add, say, `rich` for coloured tables, the
project needs a `requirements.txt` (or a `dependencies` entry in
`pyproject.toml`) and the reproducibility practices of this chapter and the
next.
:::

## Common pitfalls

::: {.callout-warning}
## Watch out
- **`pip` vs `python -m pip`**: install into the interpreter you actually run.
- **Installing into the system Python** or with `sudo`: use virtual
  environments.
- **Unpinned production dependencies**: a new release can break your
  application overnight. Pin (lock) applications; give ranges to libraries.
- **Comparing versions as strings**: `"1.10" < "1.9"`.
- **`pip freeze` in a polluted environment** exports everything you ever
  installed. Start from a clean virtual environment.
- **Ignoring resolver errors** with `--no-deps` or by forcing versions: you get
  an environment that imports but fails at run time.
:::

## Summary

- PyPI hosts third-party packages; `python -m pip` installs them (wheels
  preferred) into the current environment's `site-packages`.
- Versions follow PEP 440 and are ordered as tuples; semantic versioning gives
  meaning to MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH; specifiers (`==`, `>=`, `~=`, …) constrain
  them.
- `pip freeze > requirements.txt` exports, `pip install -r` imports; lock
  files pin the full resolved set, optionally with hashes.
- Dependency resolution is NP-complete (reduction from 3-SAT); resolvers
  backtrack with heuristics; lock files avoid repeated searching.
- Every dependency is a liability as well as an asset: choose carefully.

## Exercises

::: {#exr-ch12-spec}
Which of `1.4.0`, `1.4.5`, `1.5.0`, `2.0.0`, `1.4.5rc1` satisfy `~=1.4.1`? And
`>=1.4,!=1.4.5,<2`? Check with `packaging`.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution
`~=1.4.1` means `>=1.4.1, ==1.4.*`: only `1.4.5` (pre-releases such as
`1.4.5rc1` are excluded by default). `>=1.4,!=1.4.5,<2`: `1.4.0`, `1.5.0`.
:::

::: {#exr-ch12-semver}
A library goes from `3.7.2` to a release that (a) fixes a bug, (b) adds an
optional parameter to a function, (c) removes a deprecated function. Which
version numbers should these releases get under SemVer?
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution
(a) `3.7.3`; (b) `3.8.0`; (c) `4.0.0` — removing a public function breaks
backwards compatibility.
:::

::: {#exr-ch12-reduction}
Apply the reduction of @thm-dependency-np to the formula
$(x_1\vee x_2\vee\neg x_3)\wedge(\neg x_1\vee x_3 \vee x_2)$: list the packages,
versions and dependencies, and find an installable set.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution
Packages $X_1, X_2, X_3$ with versions 0/1; $K_1$ depends on
"$X_1{=}1 \vee X_2{=}1 \vee X_3{=}0$", $K_2$ on "$X_1{=}0\vee X_3{=}1\vee X_2{=}1$";
$T$ depends on $K_1, K_2$. Setting $x_2 = $ true satisfies both clauses:
$S = \{T, K_1, K_2, X_1{=}0, X_2{=}1, X_3{=}0\}$ (any versions of $X_1, X_3$
work).
:::
